title: Euclid's three steps past any list
hook: Name every prime there is. Euclid needs three moves to find one you missed.

knows: multiplying and dividing with a remainder
doesNotKnow: Euclid's argument that no finite list holds every prime

misconception: A long enough list of primes could be complete; or product + 1 must itself divide by one of the listed primes.
objective: The learner can say Euclid's three steps (multiply the list, add 1, divide) and why they end at a prime the list missed: every listed prime leaves remainder 1.

claims.source: Recomputed with node by trial division (Demo.tsx factor()); the stage uses the same trial division. | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node: 2·3·5·7·11·13 = 30030; 30031 = 59 × 509 by trial division (59 and 509 prime).

claims.text: For the lists 2, 3; 2, 3, 5; and 2 to 7, product + 1 is 7, 31 and 211, each prime and not on its list.
claims.source: Trial division up to the square root, recomputed with node (builder run 2026-10-14). | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node: 6 + 1 = 7, 30 + 1 = 31, 210 + 1 = 211; each is prime by trial division, and none is on its list.

claims.text: Product + 1 leaves remainder 1 when divided by each prime on the list, so none of them divides it.
claims.source: The product is a multiple of each listed p, so product + 1 = q·p + 1 with 0 < 1 < p. Stage rows show (N − 1)/p × p and r 1; checked with node for the four lists offered. | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. The product P is a multiple of each listed p, so P + 1 = qp + 1 with 0 < 1 < p, remainder 1. Own node: remainder 1 for every p on all four lists offered.

claims.text: Product + 1 is above 1, so it has a prime factor, and that prime is not on the list.
claims.source: Its smallest divisor above 1 is prime; by c3 it is not a listed prime. Shown on the stage by 'Find its primes'. | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. P + 1 >= 3 > 1, so its least divisor above 1 is prime (any smaller factor of it would divide P + 1 too), and by c3 it is not on the list. 'Find its primes' shows factor(N), which is trial division.

claims.text: Any finite list gets the same three steps, so no finite list holds every prime.
claims.source: c3 and c4 hold for any finite list of primes. Hardy and Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers, Theorem 4. | FC pass 38 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED by my own derivation (c3 and c4 use nothing about the list except that it is finite and made of primes). Hardy and Wright Theorem 4 not opened; not relied on. | FC W-2037 (fact-checker, 2026-10-25): VERIFIED against the copy edit in be3a6d58b ("no list" -> "no finite list"). Text matches Demo.tsx reveal paragraph 2 verbatim. Own derivation: for any finite list of primes p1..pk, P = p1...pk is a multiple of each pi, so P + 1 leaves remainder 1 on each (c3); P + 1 >= 2, so its least divisor above 1 is a prime, not on the list (c4). Hence no finite list of primes holds every prime. The edit narrows the conclusion to what the argument proves. Own node (BigInt trial division): remainder 1 and all prime factors off-list for every prefix list of the first 0..15 primes and for 3,5 / 2,7,13 / 5,11,17 (e.g. 16 = 2^4, 183 = 3 x 61). Hardy and Wright not opened; not relied on. | Independent fact-check 2026-10-27: company/reviews/euclid-three-steps/2026-10-27-fact-check-checks-first.md (math.euclid-three-steps.c5); exact scope and derivation/source evidence recorded there.

Its proof takes 'the least number measured by A, B, C' (for primes, their product), adds the unit, and shows that the result is prime or has a prime factor G not among A, B, C. That is the lesson's multiply, add 1, divide. The reveal 'This is Euclid's proof in the Elements, Book IX, Proposition 20' holds. recall.question: Someone claims 2, 3 and 5 are all the primes. What are Euclid's three steps, and where do they end?
options: Multiply to 30, add 1 to get 31, divide: each leaves remainder 1, so 31 brings a prime not on the list
Multiply to 30, divide by 2: 30 is even, so the list is wrong
Add them to 10, add 1 to get 11, which is prime
recall.why: Product + 1 leaves remainder 1 for every listed prime, so its own prime factors (here 31 itself) are missing from the list.
